newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf Arabs in talks to include U.S. attacks on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arabs in talks to include U.S. attacks on Iraq.

text.p: Gulf Arab foreign ministers met in Saudi Arabia on Saturday for talks which will include how to forge a response to missile strikes against Iraq by the United States, their key Western ally.

Saudi television showed foreign ministers of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain and United Arab Emirates -- seated at a round table at the start of their closed door meeting.
In an opening speech, Oman's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Youssef bin Alawi bin Abdullah said they would "discuss the most recent events in the regional and world arena."
The group planned to focus mostly on Iraq in an evening session and is expected to issue a final statement.

The six states are key allies of the United States, which used its warships deployed in the Gulf to launch missile strikes on Tuesday and Wednesday against Iraqi defence targets. Iraq said some citizens were killed in the attacks.
The United States said the missile strikes were in response to the Iraqi army's intervention in northern Iraq to help a Kurdish faction seize a city from a rival group a week ago.

The GCC said the ministers' meeting, planned before the strikes, was significant and would include latest developments in the north and south of Iraq, terrorism, ties with Iran and Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
Diplomats say there were signs of differing opinions.
"The meeting will be dominated by the U.S. attacks and how to come out with a united stand in light of the difference in opinions," one diplomat said.
Much of the Arab world has condemned the attacks as infringing on Iraq's sovereignty.
U.S. planes also fly from Saudi Arabia to patrol southern Iraq as part of a coalition with France and Britain to enforce a no-fly zone up to Iraq's 33rd parallel.

Washington decided on Tuesday to extend the zone from the 32nd parallel where it was fixed after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War. Washington says the wider zone is aimed at further restricting Iraq's ability to pose a threat to its neighbours.

"It was a very normal day," Lieutenant-Colonel Andy Bourland, public affairs director for the task force, told Reuters by telephone from Saudi Arabia when asked about Saturday's patrols. "We continue to monitor all the way up to the new extended no-fly zone for any Iraqi activity."

The GCC joined the U.S.-led multinational force that ended Iraq's 1990-91 occupation of Kuwait and supported further U.S. action against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein. Of the six states, only Kuwait has officially reacted to the latest missile strikes saying it fully understood the U.S. action.

"The opinion of some of the GCC states, especially the UAE and Qatar, is that Baghdad this time around did not threaten another country and was dealing with an internal problem. They see the U.S. attacks as unjustified," another diplomat said.

Gulf analysts say those opposed to the U.S. strikes might however stop short of openly criticising the United States, the only Western power they see capable of defending them in case of threats by their much larger neighbours, Iraq and Iran.
Iraq asked the GCC members for support.

"I urge the brethren in the Arab Gulf to take in their meeting a stand in support of Iraq against the evil and infidel forces of America," senior foreign ministry undersecretary Saad al-Faisel said in an interview carried by Iraqi state-run television on Friday.
